issue_context.title: Reduce Android 2.3 support on master (was: Investigate Android 2.3 support)
issue_context.body:
### We're already not fully supporting Android 2.3

The hard truth is we've never fully supported Android 2.3. First of all, our unit tests don't pass there in a couple of modules: http://swarm.jquery.org/job/942. There are serious AJAX issues with error handling: #1786, #2458 (#2458 seems pretty serious, see https://github.com/jquery/jquery/pull/2458#issuecomment-119572119), there are manipulation issues with checked radios: #1785.

Even though most of the tests pass, we cheat a little by putting Android 2.3 in special paths in some of them:
1. https://github.com/jquery/jquery/blob/1c59b308d201d6dd0f0aed2ad0256d01b9f68047/test/unit/ajax.js#L1507-L1512
2. https://github.com/jquery/jquery/blob/1c59b308d201d6dd0f0aed2ad0256d01b9f68047/test/unit/event.js#L408-L413
3. https://github.com/jquery/jquery/blob/1c59b308d201d6dd0f0aed2ad0256d01b9f68047/test/unit/manipulation.js#L419-L426 & https://github.com/jquery/jquery/blob/1c59b308d201d6dd0f0aed2ad0256d01b9f68047/test/unit/manipulation.js#L440-L444
4. https://github.com/jquery/jquery/blob/1c59b308d201d6dd0f0aed2ad0256d01b9f68047/test/unit/support.js#L236-L254
### Maintenance cost

There are various problems that happen only on Android 2.3, e.g. now it turns out it doesn't allow unquoted reserved words as property names, exactly as our favorite IE8: #2478. It happens quite often that something just doesn't work, e.g. currently for some reason AJAX tests hang very near the beginning: http://swarm.jquery.org/result/479018. Surprisingly, it works on `compat`: http://swarm.jquery.org/result/479031. Lots of hours are being constantly put into making this browser work with our tests.
### Market share

When we released the last stable version of jQuery, 2.1 (I'm omitting patches) [a year and a half ago](http://blog.jquery.com/2014/01/24/jquery-1-11-and-2-1-released/), Android 2.3 still had a very large market share. Currently [Google stats](http://developer.android.com/about/dashboards/index.html) show it at 5.6% of all Android versions (this is not a mobile market share but Android market share). Real percentage might be a little higher as it's counted via Google Play Store but it's still not that large as it was back then.
### Size

Cutting Android 2.3 support ([see an experimental branch that does it](https://github.com/mzgol/jquery/tree/no-android2.3)) saves 186 bytes gzipped, most of which are the `reliableMarginRight` support test and a workaround. Making all tests pass would add more.
### Resolution?

There are a couple ways to solve the problem:
1. Don't change anything, try to make Android 2.3 finally pass & continue to suffer.
2. Drop support from `master` but keep it on `compat`; still suffer, although a little less (for some reason Android 2.3 problems happen more often on `master` than `compat`).
3. Support Android 2.3 only partially - ensure it parses jQuery correctly, run a few basic tests ensuring most important APIs work on most common inputs. Don't care for perfect compliance: less suffering but such smoke testing may not be effective; also, it's hard to draw the line what's important and what's not.
4. Drop support from both branches, redirect people still needing support to the 1.x & 2.x jQuery lines.

@mzgol yes, I plan on having the meeting. The only thing that I can foresee changing that would be the fact that I'm moving this weekend, but I don't plan on letting that interfere.
Further thoughts - I think at least moving support to `compat`-only makes sense. Some bugs that appear were caused by the fact that many ES3-like workarounds are already on `compat` due to IE8 support, on `master` we discover them usually only when I look at one of recent Android 2.3 failures and discover that more things failed than usual (which is often not obvious). `compat`-only Android 2.3 support would be a little easier. Also, size difference between `2.1` & `1.11` is 50% larger than between current `master` & `compat` due to IE6-7 support removal, currently it's only 2KB gzipped: `master` weighs 29.4KB, `compat` - 32.2KB.

That's one thing; another is that I think we should restrict our Android 2.3 support slightly by saying that we won't fix non-critical bugs like sth being off-by one (a strategy we once applied e.g. to IE6 support). Note that some of the tests that currently fail on Android 2.3 look like significant breakages in some situations (like appended checked radios losing their state) and yet no one reports such things to us. I wonder if anyone noticed if we stopped working around unreliable margin right in Android 2.3.

Due to the fact that those devices are still on sale (which is so sad), I'd be ok with keeping `compat` work on Android 2.3 on a basic level - to at least ensure the library parses correctly and core APIs work, at least outside of various edge cases.

I'd like to note that Android 2.3 is broken on so many levels, many of which we cannot fix reliably that if a developer doesn't test their site on this browser, jQuery supporting it won't help; it will be broken anyway. It's easier with Android 4.0 or newer.

I'm also concerned about cases where not regressing on Android 2.3 would mean worse experience for others. Fully supporting this browser could e.g. mean we'd have to revert #1449 which would be pretty sad and would cause other issues.
After discussing this issue in the dev leads meeting, we realized something. Does anyone know of any issues with jQuery compat in hybrid apps? We've always recommended master because master didn't have the oldIE detritus, but I'm not sure we've ever actually checked to see if compat works. If it does, I think we can make Android 2.3 compat-only and recommend compat for anyone supporting 2.3 in hybrid apps.
> Does anyone know of any issues with jQuery compat in hybrid apps?

There are a couple of issues:
1. We know that Windows Modern apps are more restrictive than general web content, compare e.g. [`master`'s manipulation/support.js](https://github.com/jquery/jquery/blob/d24275372624bac897c4131fd1507a58c09a1483/src/manipulation/support.js#L11-L17) with [`compat`'s](https://github.com/jquery/jquery/blob/9c373c31410deb8e4a11aa7ce226d5e9169c7852/src/manipulation/support.js#L30-L32).
2. [`master`'s JSHint settings](https://github.com/jquery/jquery/blob/d24275372624bac897c4131fd1507a58c09a1483/src/.jshintrc#L18) declare a `window` global but don't declare the browser environment which we [do on `compat`](https://github.com/jquery/jquery/blob/9c373c31410deb8e4a11aa7ce226d5e9169c7852/src/.jshintrc#L16).
3. We don't test anything in `compat` on Node.js, on `master` we have [basic compliance tests](https://github.com/jquery/jquery/tree/master/test/node_smoke_tests).
4. There's a possibility that some of the code tailored at IE8 will cause issues, unfortunately we don't have a good way to test it apart from waiting for bug reports. Some of IE8 support tests may require changes similar to ones I described in point 1.

Obviously, we can change all that, especially points 1-3 should not be that difficult; such a change would also fix #2133. I'd be up to making these changes if that meant we could drop Android 2.3 on `master`. :D But if we say Android 2.3 support is `compat`-only, I'd like to not do even basic smoke testing of Android 2.3 on `master`.
I'd like to hold on to the Android 2.3 smoke testing in `master` so we can assert degraded support—as noted, it mostly just works and most of its specific bugs are edge cases found by us.
@gibson042 :+1:
@gibson042 What do you mean by smoke testing, though? Keeping all existing tests except maybe the ones that are currently failing or just a small set of tests checking basic API behavior?

If this would mean keeping existing tests then I don't think making Android 2.3 support officially `compat`-only would buy us that much.
Something like [ensure_iterability_es6.js](https://github.com/jquery/jquery/blob/master/test/node_smoke_tests/lib/ensure_iterability_es6.js)—load the library and use it for a handful of simple operations backed by required modules, explicitly avoiding edge cases. Support would be allowed to degrade, just not to the point where core functionality fails.
I don't think that would buy people that much, I'd guess most of the code on the web relies on at least a couple of edge cases of the API. I wouldn't oppose it too much, though, maintaining that shouldn't be a lot of trouble except the time needed for choosing proper tests initially.
Right, I'm acting on the assumption that websites will want to serve compat but native applications—or perhaps especially well-tested sites—may try master and report issues to us (a welcome change from adding code just to try fixing our unit tests).
The mobile team discussed and voted on this today and decided that in the upcoming 1.5 release we will only passively be supporting android < 4 meaning we will not remove any fixes in this version but will only be ensuring basic functionality.
Dropping Android 2.3 support won't help much unless we can also drop our super unofficial secret support for PhantomJS 1.x, since they share the same dumb limits. Can we do that yet?

Some sort of weakened Android 2.3 support as @gibson042 suggests might work, we'd just document the places where we punted because it was too hard or involved degrading support of newer and more popular browsers. 
@dmethvin

> Dropping Android 2.3 support won't help much unless we can also drop our super unofficial secret support for PhantomJS 1.x, since they share the same dumb limits.

IMO for PhantomJS 1 we mostly need workarounds for `push.apply(_, arraylike)` throwing but we need that for Android 4.0 as well anyway (it's fixed in Android > 4.0). So this needs to stay for now.

Apart from that, I don't see a lot of overlap.

> Can we do that yet?

We can't drop PhantomJS 1 yet because Mobile still relies on it; probably mostly because of https://github.com/ariya/phantomjs/issues/12948 which makes most wrapper tools still install v1.

As for Android 2.3 support itself, please see my initial post - it's not only about code size increase (although it'd be nice to rip out this ~160 bytes gzipped `reliableMarginRight` [test](https://github.com/jquery/jquery/blob/d24275372624bac897c4131fd1507a58c09a1483/src/css/support.js#L73-L99) and [workaround](https://github.com/jquery/jquery/blob/d24275372624bac897c4131fd1507a58c09a1483/src/css.js#L344-L351)) but mostly about:
1. Maintenance cost (which you might not notice because I'm usually the one to fight this stupid browser :P).
2. The fact that we've never passed the whole test suite and we do various workarounds **in tests** so that this browser more or less behaves, it's just so broken. We don't have those issues with Android 4.0+, they require some workarounds but only in source, they're able to pass the test suite which we're unable to make Android 2.3 do.

Also, (trying to) fully supporting this browser could mean reverting useful changes like #1449.
It was decided that:
1. We're adding support for non-browser environments to jQuery Compat: issue #2501, PR #2504.
2. We're cantfixing #1786 on both branches: https://github.com/jquery/jquery/issues/1786#issuecomment-125560671, https://github.com/jquery/jquery.com/issues/108.
3. We'll try to fix #1785 on `compat` only.
4. We'll maintain only basic support for Android 2.3 on `master`, meaning special tests just for this browser that don't check edge cases: issue #2505.
5. We're removing the `reliableMarginRight` support test & workaround from `master`: issue #2505.
